blocks.text: At 3 a.m. a 52-year-old man wakes with an exquisitely painful, hot, swollen big toe that cannot bear the weight of a bedsheet. Aspiration of the joint shows needle-shaped crystals that glow bright yellow and blue under polarised light. A metabolic by-product that should have been excreted has crystallised in a joint.

blocks.markdown: Tissues can accumulate abnormal deposits of minerals, crystals and pigments. This unit covers **pathological calcification** (dystrophic and metastatic), **gout** as a crystal deposition disease, and two intracellular pigments, **haemosiderin** and **lipofuscin**.

blocks.title: Pathological calcification
blocks.text: Pathological calcification is the abnormal deposition of calcium salts (mainly calcium phosphate) in tissues. It is dystrophic when it occurs in damaged or dead tissue despite normal serum calcium, and metastatic when it occurs in normal tissue because of hypercalcaemia.

rows: Atheromatous plaques, damaged or ageing heart valves (calcific aortic stenosis), necrotic tuberculous lesions, fat necrosis, infarcts
Interstitial tissues of kidneys, lungs, gastric mucosa, systemic arteries (tissues that excrete acid)
Local injury and necrosis (cell membrane damage lets calcium enter)
Hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone destruction by tumours, renal failure
Usually asymptomatic; may cause organ dysfunction (nephrocalcinosis, respiratory impairment)
blocks.caption: Dystrophic versus metastatic calcification.

blocks.markdown: In **dystrophic calcification** the calcium level in the blood is normal, so the cause is local. Dying cells and damaged mitochondria bind calcium, and membrane-derived phospholipids act as nucleation sites for calcium phosphate crystals. The deposits look like gritty, white granules and, on H&E, basophilic (blue-purple) granular material. In **metastatic calcification**, hypercalcaemia (or, less often, high phosphate) drives deposition into otherwise healthy tissues, in particular those that lose acid and become relatively alkaline (gastric mucosa, kidney tubules, pulmonary alveolar walls). Causes of hypercalcaemia include primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D intoxication, destruction of bone (metastases, multiple myeloma) and sarcoidosis, and chronic renal failure with secondary hyperparathyroidism.

blocks.title: Classify the calcification
blocks.prompt: (a) A 78-year-old has a stenotic aortic valve with calcified nodules. Serum calcium is normal. (b) A 40-year-old woman with a parathyroid adenoma has serum calcium 3.4 mmol/L (reference ranges vary by laboratory; roughly 2.2 to 2.6) and calcium deposits in the renal tubules and lungs. Classify each.

steps.text: (a) Damaged, degenerate valve tissue with normal serum calcium: dystrophic calcification.
(b) Normal tissues with a raised serum calcium from excess parathyroid hormone: metastatic calcification.
The discriminator is the serum calcium level and the state of the tissue.

blocks.markdown:
### Gout as a crystal deposition disease

Gout results from **hyperuricaemia** and deposition of **monosodium urate (MSU) crystals** in joints and soft tissues. Uric acid is the end product of purine catabolism in humans (xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid); it is excreted mainly by the kidney. Hyperuricaemia arises from **overproduction** (high purine turnover, as in cell lysis with chemotherapy, myeloproliferative disease; enzyme defects such as HGPRT deficiency in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) or, more commonly, **reduced renal excretion** (renal impairment, diuretics, low-dose aspirin), often with a dietary and genetic contribution. When the urate level exceeds its solubility in the body fluids (limited at lower temperatures and in acid conditions), crystals precipitate in the joint.

The crystals are phagocytosed by neutrophils and macrophages and activate the **NLRP3 inflammasome**, which releases **interleukin-1 beta** and drives intense acute inflammation (**acute gouty arthritis**, classically of the first metatarsophalangeal joint). Repeated attacks and persistent deposition lead to **tophi** (masses of urate crystals surrounded by a granulomatous reaction in joints, cartilage, tendons and ear helix) and chronic arthritis and renal damage (urate nephropathy and stones). Aspirated crystals are **needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent** under polarised light, appearing yellow when parallel to the axis of the compensator. This contrasts with pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystals, rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent).

blocks.title: From purines to the painful toe
blocks.prompt: Explain why a patient on a thiazide diuretic who drinks heavy beer and eats large amounts of red meat develops gout.

steps.text: Dietary purines and alcohol raise urate production, while thiazide diuretics and alcohol reduce renal urate excretion: serum urate rises.
When urate exceeds its solubility (cooler peripheral joints such as the big toe favour crystallisation), MSU crystals precipitate.
Phagocytes ingest crystals and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1 beta. Neutrophils are recruited, causing acute pain, redness and swelling.
Joint fluid shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.

blocks.answer: Hyperuricaemia leads to MSU crystal deposition and an IL-1-driven acute inflammatory arthritis.

blocks.markdown:
### Intracellular pigments

**Haemosiderin** is a golden-yellow to brown granular pigment derived from haemoglobin, representing aggregates of ferritin that store iron. It forms when there is local or systemic excess of iron. It stains **blue with Prussian blue** (Perls stain) because of ferric iron. Local excess occurs after haemorrhage (a bruise changes colour from red-blue to green to yellow-brown as haemoglobin is converted to biliverdin, bilirubin and haemosiderin) and in chronic pulmonary congestion (haemosiderin-laden macrophages, 'heart failure cells'). Systemic overload (**haemosiderosis**) occurs after repeated transfusions or increased absorption; if it damages organs (liver, heart, pancreas) it is **haemochromatosis**, with cirrhosis, diabetes and heart failure.

**Lipofuscin** ('wear and tear' pigment) is a yellow-brown, finely granular pigment composed of lipid-protein complexes from oxidative damage to cell membranes and organelles (lipid peroxidation), accumulating in lysosomes of long-lived, non-dividing or slowly dividing cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes). It is a marker of past free-radical injury and cell ageing and is **not harmful** to the cell; extreme accumulation gives *brown atrophy* of the heart and liver.

rows: Breakdown of haemoglobin (stored iron as ferritin aggregates)
Oxidised lipid-protein residue from membrane peroxidation
Bruising, pulmonary congestion, haemochromatosis, transfusion overload
Ageing, brown atrophy of heart and liver
Marker of iron excess; toxic in large amounts
Marker of past oxidative injury; benign
blocks.caption: Comparison of two intracellular pigments.

items: Dystrophic calcification: normal calcium, damaged tissue; metastatic: high calcium, normal tissue.
Gout crystals: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate.
Lipofuscin accumulates with age in neurons, myocytes and hepatocytes.

blocks.title: Do not mix up the crystals
blocks.text: Gout is monosodium urate (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent); pseudogout is calcium pyrophosphate (rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent). Both cause acute arthritis, but the crystal differs and so does the management.

points: Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or damaged tissue with normal serum calcium; metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue when serum calcium is raised.
Gout is caused by hyperuricaemia and deposition of monosodium urate crystals that activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta, causing acute arthritis and tophi.
Haemosiderin is an iron-containing pigment from haemoglobin that stains with Prussian blue; lipofuscin is a benign wear-and-tear pigment from oxidative damage that accumulates with age.

questions.stem: Which condition is an example of dystrophic calcification?

options.text: Calcification in an atheromatous plaque in a normocalcaemic patient
Calcium deposits in the gastric mucosa due to vitamin D toxicity
Pulmonary calcification in hypercalcaemia from myeloma

questions.correctOptionText: Calcification in an atheromatous plaque in a normocalcaemic patient
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or necrotic tissue such as atheroma despite normal serum calcium. The other options reflect hypercalcaemia acting on normal tissue.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism has calcium deposits in lung and gastric mucosa. Why are these tissues favoured?

options.text: They excrete acid and become relatively alkaline, favouring precipitation of calcium salts

questions.correctOptionText: They excrete acid and become relatively alkaline, favouring precipitation of calcium salts
questions.explanation: Tissues that lose acid have a relatively alkaline interior, which promotes calcium phosphate precipitation when calcium or phosphate is raised.

questions.stem: Joint aspirate from a hot swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint shows needle-shaped crystals that are strongly negatively birefringent. Which substance is responsible?

distractorRationale.d: A pigment, not a crystal in joint fluid.

questions.explanation: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals are monosodium urate, diagnostic of gout. Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

questions.stem: Which cytokine, released after the NLRP3 inflammasome is activated by urate crystals, is the main driver of the acute inflammation in gout?
questions.explanation: Phagocytosed urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and release IL-1 beta, which recruits neutrophils and produces acute inflammation.

questions.stem: A section of lung from a patient with chronic left heart failure contains macrophages with golden-brown cytoplasmic granules that stain blue with Perls stain. These are:
questions.explanation: Prussian blue positivity identifies iron in haemosiderin. In chronic pulmonary congestion red cells leak into alveoli and are phagocytosed, producing these 'heart failure cells'.

questions.stem: True or false: Lipofuscin is a harmful pigment that directly causes cell death.
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is an indicator of past oxidative damage and ageing and is not itself toxic. Extreme accumulation produces brown atrophy without cell death.

questions.stem: A man with gout has a serum urate concentration of 0.52 mmol/L. Taking the approximate solubility limit of urate in plasma at body temperature as 0.40 mmol/L, calculate by what percentage his urate exceeds this limit. Values are for teaching and laboratory limits vary.
questions.explanation: The excess is (0.52 - 0.40)/0.40 = 0.30, i.e. 30% above the solubility limit. Supersaturation favours crystal precipitation, especially in cooler peripheral joints.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperparathyroidism has serum total calcium of 3.2 mmol/L and a serum phosphate of 1.5 mmol/L. Calculate the calcium-phosphate product in mmol^2/L^2.
questions.explanation: Product = 3.2 x 1.5 = 4.8 mmol^2/L^2. A raised calcium-phosphate product promotes precipitation of calcium salts in normal tissue, the basis of metastatic calcification.

questions.stem: Differentiate dystrophic from metastatic calcification, giving the serum calcium status, tissue state, mechanism and two examples of each.
markingGuide: Dystrophic: damaged or dead tissue, normal serum calcium, local nucleation on damaged membranes
Dystrophic examples: atheroma, calcific aortic stenosis, tuberculous necrosis, fat necrosis
Metastatic: normal tissue, hypercalcaemia (or high phosphate)
Metastatic mechanism: precipitation in alkaline, acid-excreting tissues (kidney, lung, stomach)
Metastatic causes: hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone destruction, renal failure
questions.explanation: The key distinction is whether the tissue or the serum calcium is abnormal. Each has typical causes and sites.

questions.stem: Describe the pathogenesis of gout from hyperuricaemia to acute arthritis and tophus formation.
markingGuide: Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism; hyperuricaemia from overproduction or reduced renal excretion
Supersaturation leads to monosodium urate crystal precipitation in joints (favoured by cooler temperatures)
Phagocytosis of crystals activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release
Neutrophil recruitment causes acute gouty arthritis
Chronic deposition forms tophi with granulomatous reaction; renal complications
Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals in aspirate
questions.explanation: Crystal formation is the trigger, and the innate immune response produces the symptoms.
